key_insight: A single deep model jointly predicts bioactivity and reconstructs molecules to produce a principled, actionable measure of distribution shift—enabling discovery of active kinase inhibitors at the edge of chemical space.
problem_solved: Addresses unreliable generalization and lack of principled out‑of‑distribution detection in molecular ML, which hinders prioritization of novel chemotypes for experimental testing.
method: Train a unified model that reconstructs molecules (autoencoding/generative objective) and simultaneously predicts bioactivity (supervised head) from a shared latent space.
Derive a principled distribution‑shift score from reconstruction/latent statistics to quantify how far a query molecule lies from training data.
Prospectively validate by prioritizing compounds with favorable predicted activity and shift scores, experimentally discovering active inhibitors for two kinases.
impact: Provides a practical approach to quantify and manage distribution shift in molecular models, improving trust, prioritization, and success rates when moving from in‑silico predictions to experimental validation.
visual_elements: Model schematic: encoder → latent space → decoder (reconstruction) + predictor (bioactivity) with annotated loss terms
Chemical‑space map (UMAP/t‑SNE) showing training set vs. candidate compounds colored by distribution‑shift score and experimental activity
Scatter plot: distribution‑shift score vs. predicted activity highlighting experimentally confirmed actives
Pipeline diagram: in‑silico prioritization → selection by shift score → in vitro kinase assays (prospective validation)
paper_title: Molecular deep learning at the edge of chemical space
paper_authors: Derek van Tilborg, Luke Rossen, Francesca Grisoni
